transcript.text: I am the product manager of a travel booking site. We want to know whether offering free cancellation makes fewer people cancel, so we can decide whether to offer it on every trip. The table I shared is our bookings: when each was booked, the travel date, destination, channel, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Today free cancellation is offered on some trips and not on others; partners and our pricing team choose which, nobody assigned it at random. Tell me what you would do to answer this. [shares bookings.csv]

What I understand: you run a travel booking site, free cancellation is already offered on some trips (chosen by partners and your pricing team, not at random), and you want to know if offering it on every trip would reduce cancellations, using bookings.csv (1,500 bookings with booking and travel dates, destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free cancellation flag, and cancelled flag).

The real problem is causal, not descriptive: because free cancellation was never assigned at random, a simple comparison of cancellation rates between trips with and without it would likely reflect who chose it rather than what it does. What I still need to know before the final number matters: will you decide based on the cancellation rate alone, or do you also need to know what free cancellation does to revenue or profit (refunds, costs)?

Here is what I would do:

1. Compare cancellation rates between free-cancellation and non-free bookings, split by destination, channel, price band, lead time, and booking date, so we can see how different the two groups are and where the confounding lives. It needs only your table, which we have. The step is done when the breakdown is visible; we should expect the raw comparison to be misleading.

2. Adjust for confounding by modeling cancelled on free_cancellation while controlling for destination, channel, price, lead_time_days, nationality, and the booking and travel dates — either a regression or propensity-score matching/weighting — to isolate the effect of offering free cancellation. It needs no new data. It is checked by whether the treated and control groups look balanced after adjustment and whether the estimate stays stable across model choices; stop when the estimate stops moving much.

3. Stress-test the result by checking whether the effect holds within each segment or whether one segment drives it. It is checked by segment-level estimates; stop when the picture is consistent enough to support a decision.

One question: will you decide based on the cancellation rate alone, or do you also need to know what free cancellation does to revenue or profit?

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)
Everything I know is in what I wrote. Choose what you judge best and go ahead.

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table above this message]

I'll go with a stratified analysis: compare cancellation rates between free-cancellation and non-free bookings overall and within destination, channel, price, and lead-time segments. This shows the raw difference and how much it shifts when we account for the factors partners and pricing use to choose — the best we can do with observational data, since free cancellation wasn't randomly assigned and the table can't show financial impact.

Here is what the bookings show. Overall, cancelled bookings are 23.3% among free-cancellation trips (623 bookings) versus 22.6% among non-free-cancellation trips (877 bookings) — so the raw comparison actually runs the wrong way. But it flips by segment: free cancellation pairs with lower cancellation on the app (20.3% vs 24.2%) and through agents (23.0% vs 24.4%) and in Paris (18.2% vs 19.5%), yet with higher cancellation in Bangkok (28.6% vs 21.9%) and on the web (25.2% vs 20.9%). Price could not be grouped because it is stored as an identifier, and lead time was not broken out. What this means: because free cancellation was never assigned at random — partners and your pricing team choose which trips get it — this raw comparison is confounded. The segment pattern changing direction across destination and channel is exactly the signature of that confounding. The table alone cannot isolate the true effect of free cancellation, and it contains no cost or revenue data, so it cannot show whether offering it everywhere is worth it financially. To go further, I would adjust for the confounders — destination, channel, price band, lead time, and booking/travel dates — using a regression or propensity-score approach, which sits outside what simple table queries can do.

transcript.text: I lead retention at a subscription company. I want a model that tells us, for each customer, which discount to offer (none, 10 percent or 25 percent) so that they do not leave. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. We have never given discounts before, so there is no record of any offer or of how customers reacted. The retention team would use the result every month. [shares customers.csv]

Thank you — your table is confirmed: 1,200 customers with segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets, and a churn flag. Let me record what I've understood and lay out honest options.

Here's what I understood and how I'd approach it.

**What the problem really is.** You want to pick, for each customer every month, one of three discounts (none, 10%, 25%) so they don't churn. Your table only records what happened when no discount was offered — every customer's churn flag reflects the no-discount condition, and there's no record of who received an offer or how they reacted. So the obvious idea — training a model to predict "which discount works" — can't be done from this history alone. What we *can* learn is who is likely to churn without any discount.

**My approach.** Rather than pretend we can predict discount response from data that has none, I'd start with what's actually learnable: a churn-risk model that scores every customer, so the retention team knows whom to prioritize. Separately, a small randomized pilot (none / 10% / 25%) would let you learn which discount actually works, and later build a true recommendation model. The risk model gives you something to act on now; the pilot is what makes the discount recommendation possible.

**Plan:**
1. Build a churn-risk model from segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, and support tickets to predict churned_next_month.
2. Score and rank all 1,200 customers by churn risk so the team can prioritize outreach each month.
3. (Optional) Design a randomized discount pilot for next month's at-risk customers, then convert the results into a per-customer discount recommendation.

Here are three ways to proceed. They differ in what they give you and how quickly.

choices.title: Churn-risk model + risk-ranked discount targeting
choices.what: Train a model to predict each customer's chance of churning next month from segment, plan, tenure, spend, and support tickets. Rank all 1,200 customers by risk so the retention team knows whom to prioritize for a discount. You get: A monthly churn-risk score per customer, plus the factors driving risk (segment, plan, tenure_months, monthly_spend, support_tickets_90d). Trade-off: Tells you who is likely to leave, but not which discount level will save them — you'd choose one discount level as a business rule since no discount history exists. Effort: Moderate (a few days).

choices.title: Discount-response experiment design
choices.what: Design a randomized pilot: similar customers are randomly offered none, 10%, or 25% off next month, with defined group sizes and a success metric (who stayed, was the discount worth it). You get: A ready-to-run experiment plan and, after the pilot, the data to build a true per-customer discount recommendation model. Trade-off: You learn what actually works, but you wait one month for results and some customers receive discounts that turn out not to be best for them. Effort: Low to moderate.

choices.title: Current churn-pattern analysis
choices.what: Aggregate churn by segment, city, plan, tenure, and support tickets to see which groups leave most right now. You get: A snapshot of where churn is concentrated, with numbers you can act on immediately without modeling. Trade-off: No per-customer model and no discount recommendation — just insight for manual targeting. Effort: Low.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a travel agency. I want to predict, at the moment a booking is made, whether it will be cancelled, so the operations team can overbook the right trips. The table I shared is our bookings up to late February 2026: booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Some of the trips in it have not happened yet. Operations would score every new booking once, on the day it is made. [shares bookings.csv]

No column leaks the cancellation outcome, which is good since scoring must use only what's known at booking time. Let me record what I've understood and lay out options.

I understood the problem like this: at the moment a booking is made, you want to know whether it will be cancelled, so the operations team can overbook the trips where cancellations are most likely. Each new booking is scored once, on its booking day. I've recorded your goal, the overbooking decision, and that operations is the user. My working assumptions: cancelled is a 0/1 flag; any booking whose travel date hasn't arrived yet has no known outcome and stays out of training; scoring uses only information known on the booking date. I checked the ten feature columns against the outcome and found none that leak the answer.

Approach: rather than modelling all rows at once, I'd use a time-based holdout — train on older bookings, validate on newer ones — so the model is tested the way it will actually be used, scoring future bookings from information available at booking time. This beats the obvious option of using everything available or including post-booking details, which would overstate accuracy.

Plan:
1. Build the labelled set: keep bookings with a known cancelled value, dropping trips whose travel date hasn't happened yet, and confirm cancelled is 0/1. Needs: the table. Checked by row counts before and after. Stop if too few bookings are labelled.
2. Build booking-day features only (destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free cancellation) and re-verify no leakage. Needs: the column list. Checked by a leakage re-check. Stop if a clean feature set exists.
3. Train the model on older bookings and evaluate on a recent holdout, measuring how well it ranks high-risk bookings. Needs: cancelled as the outcome. Checked by holdout metrics. Stop if performance is usable.
4. Convert the probability into an overbooking rule with operations' costs (empty seat vs. denied boarding). Needs: cost inputs you don't have in the table. Checked by a threshold policy. Stop if operations can apply it.

Which direction fits best — the prediction model, the cancellation analysis, or the business overbooking rule? Once you pick, I'll say what DCLab would build and ask once whether to go ahead.

choices.title: Build a booking-time cancellation prediction model
choices.what: DCLab trains a model on bookings whose outcome is already known, using only information available on the booking date — destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free cancellation — and validates with a time-based holdout so it behaves like scoring a new booking today. You get: A model that returns a cancellation probability for every new booking, plus holdout metrics showing how well it ranks high-risk bookings, so operations can choose which trips to overbook. Trade-off: It predicts risk but does not set the overbooking number itself — you still need a cost rule (empty seat vs. denied boarding) to turn probability into how many extra bookings to accept, and it assumes future bookings look like past ones. Effort: Moderate — one model build with a holdout check.

choices.title: Measure where cancellations happen now (analysis)
choices.what: DCLab computes the overall cancellation rate and breaks it down by destination, channel, lead time, and free cancellation, plus how the rate changes over booking date. You get: Numbers showing which segments lose the most bookings to cancellation and whether cancellation risk is rising over time. Trade-off: Describes the past only; it won't score a future booking or tell operations how much to overbook. Effort: Light — a few aggregate queries.

choices.title: Turn risk into an overbooking rule (business brief)
choices.what: DCLab translates a cancellation probability into an accept-overbook rule using the cost of an empty seat versus the cost of turning a customer away, and lists what cost inputs you'd need from operations. You get: A threshold policy (e.g., overbook when predicted cancellation probability × seat value exceeds denied-boarding cost) and the list of missing cost inputs. Trade-off: Needs cost numbers the table doesn't contain; works best once the prediction model exists, though it can start from today's average cancellation rate. Effort: Light.
